quote: What's got you looking at solar for the home?
stewart_read: The rep asks the interest question early and gets a real answer, but the answer ('just thinking about it, see how much... I'm looking at') is filed and never revisited — no depth probe, no follow-up on what would make the numbers compelling.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged the answer too thin to expand on and moved to qualify faster, which is a defensible efficiency call on a low-urgency lead.
coaching_implication: Coach a one-line depth follow-up ('what would make solar worth it for you — is it more about the monthly cost or just curiosity?') even on soft answers; it gives the closer a real anchor instead of a placeholder.

stewart_read: Bill range is captured cleanly and confirmed back ('$1.50 to 200. Got that here'), satisfying the capture half of bill_anchoring, but there is no flip into emotional alignment-against-the-utility at this point in the call.
coaching_implication: Model the ask+acknowledge+flip pattern — after confirming the bill range, name what that adds up to annually or seasonally to make the number land as pain, not just data.

quote: Yeah. I can see that's probably where those 200 bills are at here. July and August is pretty high.
stewart_read: This is the moment the bill should have been flipped — the rep has the actual bill on screen and names the seasonal spike, but immediately pivots to internal process ('I'll get all of this sent over to my design team') instead of using the spike as leverage.
coaching_implication: This is the flip point the manager should replay: pause on 'so in the summer you're paying $200+ for power you could be paying a flat, lower solar payment for' before moving to scheduling.

quote: You cannot just send it to me through email or something?
stewart_read: This is a direct trigger for the hard rule and the rep holds it correctly rather than caving, which is the schema-compliant outcome (held_line_with_improvisation).
alternative_hypothesis: Could be read as a partial cave since the rep does agree to email a copy afterward, but the transcript shows the walkthrough is preserved as the primary appointment — the concession is only for a post-call record.
coaching_implication: Reinforce this as a good example for the rep — she protected the appointment's value while still answering the customer's underlying want (a copy for records).

quote: One okay. 1PM then I mean, do they call pretty much, on the dot on time or there is a
stewart_read: Customer's fragmented question about call punctuality signals scheduling anxiety tied to his stated changing plans; the rep answers with a firm window ('We usually call within five minutes') which is a reasonable anchor, but does not re-confirm the exact final time split between 1:00 and 1:30 that the customer verbalized.
coaching_implication: Manager should note the ambiguity ('I'll put it between one, 01:30') was never explicitly resolved back to a single locked time — worth a clean re-confirmation before ending calls with a hedge like this.

quote: Perfect. K. Alright. Well, both of them. I'll get everything scheduled.
stewart_read: When the rep realizes she doesn't have the customer's email on file ('I actually don't have one on file here. Can I grab that?'), she admits the gap transparently and recovers immediately rather than faking it or skipping it — a clean example of admit-and-recover.
coaching_implication: This is a positive, reusable model — flag it to the rep as the right way to handle a data gap live on a call: name it, ask for it, move on without breaking flow.

quote: K. Alright. Well, both of them. I'll get everything scheduled. We'll plan on calling you tomorrow at one.
stewart_read: The button-up is incomplete against schema requirements: the rep confirms day and time ('tomorrow at one') but never states the one-hour block, never gives the no-driving/at-computer instruction, and never runs the 'is that fair?' verbal handshake. Since this appointment is a phone call rather than an in-person design review, the no-driving/at-computer language is still schema-relevant — the design review happens over the phone while the customer should be seated and available, not just the general instruction being 'less applicable.'
alternative_hypothesis: One could argue phone appointments need a lighter button-up than in-person ones, but the schema ties the no-driving/at-computer instruction specifically to reviewing the design, which still occurs on this call regardless of channel.
coaching_implication: Coach the full button_up sequence as a checklist regardless of channel: state the hour block, tell the customer to be seated and not driving, and close with 'is that fair?' — this call books cleanly but skips three of the four confirmation elements that protect show rate.
